newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - BMW warns 97 sales growth set to slow.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BMW warns 97 sales growth set to slow.

text.p: MUNICH, Germany, March 25 - German luxury carmaker BMW, which had one of the most successful years in its history in 1996, warned on Tuesday that sales growth was about to slow.

Bayerische Motoren Werke AG chairman Bernd Pischetsrieder told the company's annual press conference that sluggish global markets and limited capacity at BMW group plants left little room for the company to improve on its 13.3 percent sales growth last year.
"We are very confident about 1997," Pischetsrieder said. "But we will not see the same order of magnitude of sales growth this year."
BMW group sales, fuelled by the hot-selling 5-Series executive class saloon and the Z3 sports car, appeared to start 1997 in high gear, climbing 22 percent to 14 billion marks ($8.3 billion).
But the car company said that a combination of fundamental factors and a statistical one-off will dampen growth as the year goes on.

The world's major car markets face a difficult year in 1997, BMW said. Tax advantages that fuelled demand for new cars in some European countries have been abolished and slow real income growth has left consumers with less money for BMW's luxury cars.
Markets in the United States and Japan, two of the most important for BMW, are expected to stagnate, the company said.
"After the strong growth of 1996, BMW sales are likely to stabilise at the current high level," BMW said.
Pischetsrieder added that even if demand was better than expected, the company would have little room to increase production as its plants are already running near capacity.
A sharp increase in first quarter sales this year, meanwhile, should not be taken at face value.
The BMW chairman said much of the gain was due to the fact that the company's two new models were not available over all of 1996.

"It is important to consider the base effect of the engine and model change-overs at the beginning of last year," Pischetsrieder said. "The growth rates are very high at the moment, but are expected to diminish, in percent terms, in coming months."
Another question mark hanging over BMW sales this year is the timing of the launch of a new 3-Series model -- BMW's backbone car, accounting for about two thirds of BMW brand sales.
Car industry analysts expect demand for the car, introduced in 1991, to slow this year as consumers hold off buying a new car until they can have the latest offering from Munich.
Pressed about the launch of the new model, BMW executives would only say it would not be introduced this year and that the company historically only changes models about every seven to eight years.

Pischetsrieder generally refused to provide a specific sales forecast for 1997, but when asked by a reporter if 60 billion marks was possible, he simply answered "yes." Group sales in 1996 were worth 52.27 billion marks.

With limited room to expand sales, BMW aims to increase its earnings power by cutting the amount of red ink at two money-losing operations -- its British unit Rover Group and its aircraft engine unit BMW Rolls-Royce GmbH.

In 1996, Rover posted a 279 million mark loss in pre-tax ordinary activities, down from a 335 million mark loss the year before. The aircraft engine unit, meanwhile, posted a 627 million mark loss after last year's 652 million mark loss.

BMW brought Rover in 1994 and is pumping billions of marks into the company in the hope of seeing it turn a profit by 2000. In 1996 alone, BMW invested 1.2 billion marks in Rover and plans another 600 million pounds of investment this year.
The BMW Rolls-Royce venture is also starting to deliver its first engines for Britain's luxury Rolls-Royce cars, boosting revenue.
BMW said 1996 profit, according to the widely-used German DVFA accounting standard, rose to 959 million marks from 795 million. ($ = 1.686 German Marks)
